lines.text: Philippians 3: 7-14
But whatever gain I had, I counted as loss for the sake of
Christ. Indeed I count everything as loss because of the surpass-
ing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord. For his sake I
have suffered the loss of all things, and count them as refuse, in
order that I may gain Christ and be found in him, not having
a righteousness of my own, based on law, but that which is
through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God that depends
on faith; that I may know him and the power of his resurrection,
and may share his sufferings, becoming like him in his death,
that if possible I may attain the resurrection from the dead.
Not that I have already obtained this or am already perfect;
but I press on to make it my own, because Christ Jesus has
made me his own. Brethren, I do not consider that I have
made it my own; but one thing I do, forgetting what lies behind
and straining forward to what lies ahead, I press on toward the
goal for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus.
I
At the end of a term we look both backwards and forwards.
Yet, are we right to look back? Paul says: "
... forgetting
what lies behind and straining forward to what lies
ahead. ..." Yet Paul too looks back. He remembers the
great things that God has done for him, that he was gripped
by the vision of Jesus Christ and that in consequence he
counted his former gain as loss.
In what sense then shall we feel it right to look back, and
in what sense shall we feel that we ought not to? The
"forgetting" of which Paul speaks does not mean that he
banishes the past from his mind, letting bygones be bygones;
it means that he makes a discriminating judgment with
regard to the past. He surrenders everything that the past,
as such, contained which might tempt him to be proud, to
